function: Deep Q-learning policy decides how many RIS elements and which positions each user pair receives per frame, maximizing sum-rate under inter-user interference (p. 3-4, 6).
system: Passive reflecting RIS, 8x8=64 elements (M=16 in quantization study), 3 or 4 user pairs, no direct path, Rician block fading; antennas, band not stated (p. 1, 3, 7, 9).
method: Deep Q-learning policy network (epsilon-greedy, target network, Bellman loss), reward = weighted user throughput minus weighted interference; online reinforcement learning, 5,000 training episodes (p. 5-7).
data_channel: Own simulated environment: i.i.d. Rician block-fading uplink and downlink links, random user distances up to 100 m, no direct path; no dataset or measurements (p. 3, 6).
test_conditions: Trained 5,000 episodes, converging near 3,000, with 8x8 RIS; results shown for 3 and 4 users and SINR versus quantization bits; no unseen-condition test reported (p. 7-9).
baselines: Uniform RIS-element allocation strategy of [6] (Fig. 12), non-learned; no learned baseline compared (p. 9-10).
metrics: Per-user achievable rate and sum-rate versus episodes, rate against uniform allocation, average SINR and phase-error variance versus quantization bits, normalized allocation distributions, overhead curve (p. 7-10).
complexity: none; only a signaling-overhead curve (Fig. 11) and 5,000 training episodes are given (p. 7, 9-10).
q1_support: p. 3: "All links are independent, identically distributed, and Rician faded." The environment is "a custom-built environment that models dynamic channel fading" (p. 3); no 3GPP, QuaDRiGa, DeepMIMO, COST 2100 or measured channel is used.
q2_support: p. 7: "We employed an 8×8 RIS with 64 elements. The number of users considered for the analysis are 3 and 4 in a multi-cell environment." Both cases are separate analyses in the same simulator; p. 3: "is independent of the number of users" is a design claim, and no model trained in one setting is tested in another.
q3_support: p. 9: "The performance of our proposed method with that of the uniform allocation strategy reported in [6] is compared" (Fig. 12). That is a non-learned baseline only; no earlier learned method for the same function is compared, since the Q-learning policy is the proposed method itself.
q4_support: p. 9: "requires a low amount of control signaling to configure the RIS elements" is signaling overhead alone; no order of complexity, operations, parameters or runtime of the method is reported (p. 7 gives only the GPU and the 5,000 training episodes).
q5_support: p. 3: "a custom-built environment that models dynamic channel fading" is the only data source; no code or data link or DOI appears anywhere in the paper, and no public channel dataset or measurement is used.
notes: Include; page 1 holds the title iRIS: A Deep Policy Learning Framework for Intelligent Distribution of RIS Elements, matching the DOI. Area 3: the learned deep Q-policy chooses the number and positions of RIS elements assigned to each user pair, with phases and positions as variables of the sum-rate problem (p. 4), which is RIS configuration, not above-PHY scheduling. RIS is passive (p. 1). Jain's fairness index is defined (p. 6) but no fairness result is plotted, and the text calls the overhead result Fig. 12 although the overhead curve is Fig. 11 (p. 9-10). All five criteria are 0.
